title: The First-Kind Companion to the Bell Row Sum
content: **Framing.** The unsigned Stirling number of the first kind $c(n, k) = \mathtt{Nat.stirlingFirst}\,n\,k$ counts the permutations of an $n$-element set with exactly $k$ disjoint cycles. Conditioning on the cycle count partitions *all* $n!$ permutations, so summing the parts recovers the total: $\sum_{k=0}^{n} c(n, k) = n!$. This is the first-kind mirror of the second-kind identity $\sum_k S(n, k) = B_n$ (Bell number) developed in the parent `bell-numbers-oq-01` family. Pinned Mathlib carries $\mathtt{Nat.stirlingFirst}$ with its triangular recurrence and boundary values, but *not* this row sum — the gap this entry fills.
mathContext: Set $x = 1$ in the rising-factorial identity $x(x+1)\cdots(x+n-1) = \sum_k c(n,k)\,x^k$: the left side becomes $n!$, giving $\sum_k c(n,k) = n!$.
relatedConcepts: Cycle-count interpretation of the first-kind Stirling numbers
prerequisites: The symmetric group S_n and its cycle decomposition

title: The Vanishing Boundary Lemma n·c(n,0) = 0
content: **The bookkeeping key.** `mul_stirlingFirst_zero`: $n \cdot c(n, 0) = 0$ for every $n$. Case split on $n$: at $n = 0$ the leading factor kills the product (`simp`); for $n \ge 1$, `Nat.stirlingFirst_succ_zero` gives $c(n, 0) = 0$. The subtlety is that $c(0, 0) = 1 \ne 0$, so the *bare* value $c(n, 0)$ is not uniformly zero — but the factor $n$ makes the *product* vanish everywhere. This is exactly what lets the $k = 0$ term dropped during the re-index be reinstated for free, since it always reappears multiplied by $n$.
mathContext: $c(n, 0) = [n = 0]$, so $n \cdot c(n, 0) = n \cdot [n = 0] = 0$ — the one place the first-kind boundary differs from a clean zero, neutralised by the factor $n$.

title: The Recurrence Collapse: Σ c(n,k) = n!
content: **The centrepiece.** `stirlingFirst_row_sum`: $\sum_{k \in \mathrm{range}(n+1)} c(n, k) = n!$, proved by induction on $n$. Absent from pinned Mathlib, which records only boundary values of `stirlingFirst`. The base case $n = 0$ is $c(0,0) = 0! = 1$ (`simp`); the whole content is in the inductive step, which turns the triangular recurrence into the one-step factorial recurrence $(n+1)! = (n+1)\cdot n!$. Strategically: the $(n+1)$-st row sum splits, via $c(n+1, k+1) = n\,c(n, k+1) + c(n, k)$, into $n(\sum_k c(n, k+1)) + (\sum_k c(n, k))$; the second summand is the induction hypothesis $n!$ and the first re-indexes back to $n\cdot n!$, giving $(n+1)\,n!$.
mathContext: $\sum_k c(n{+}1, k) = n\,n! + n! = (n+1)\,n! = (n+1)!$ — the triangular recurrence turns the row sum into a one-step factorial recurrence.
prerequisites: the row-sum statement of the companion identity

title: Peel, re-index, and collapse the inductive step
content: **The mechanics of the step.** Four moves close it. (1) Peel the $k=0$ term of the $(n+1)$-st row with `sum_range_succ'`; it vanishes since $c(n+1,0)=0$ (`stirlingFirst_succ_zero`), and each remaining $c(n+1,i+1)$ is expanded by `stirlingFirst_succ_succ`. (2) `sum_add_distrib` + `mul_sum` distribute to $n(\sum_i c(n,i+1)) + (\sum_i c(n,i))$; the right summand is the IH $n!$. (3) The re-index lemma `hsplit` proves $(\sum_i c(n,i+1)) + c(n,0) = n!$ — a shifted sum plus its dropped boundary term reassemble the full $n$-th row, with `stirlingFirst_eq_zero_of_lt` killing the out-of-range top term $c(n,n+1)$. (4) Multiply `hsplit` by $n$ and erase $n\cdot c(n,0)$ via `mul_stirlingFirst_zero`, yielding $n(\sum_i c(n,i+1)) = n\cdot n!$; then `Nat.factorial_succ` + `ring` finish $(n+1)\,n! = (n+1)!$. The dropped boundary term costs nothing precisely because it always reappears multiplied by $n$.
mathContext: $\bigl(\textstyle\sum_i c(n,i{+}1)\bigr) + c(n,0) = n!$ and $n\cdot c(n,0) = 0$, so $n\bigl(\textstyle\sum_i c(n,i{+}1)\bigr) = n\cdot n!$, whence $n\cdot n! + n! = (n+1)!$.
relatedConcepts: reinstating a dropped boundary term via the factor n

title: The Combinatorial Content: Equals the Permutation Count
content: **Promoting arithmetic to combinatorics.** `stirlingFirst_row_sum_eq_card_perm`: $\sum_{k \in \mathrm{range}(n+1)} c(n, k) = |\mathrm{Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)|$. Rewrite the row sum to $n!$ (previous theorem), then `Fintype.card_perm` ($|\mathrm{Perm}\,\alpha| = (\mathrm{card}\,\alpha)!$) and `Fintype.card_fin` ($\mathrm{card}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n) = n$) turn $n!$ into $|\mathrm{Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)|$. This makes explicit that the $c(n, k)$ are a genuine partition of the $n!$ permutations by cycle count — the left side sorts them by cycle count, the right counts them all at once.
mathContext: $\sum_k c(n, k) = |\mathrm{Perm}(\mathrm{Fin}\,n)| = n!$: the row sum is the count of the symmetric group, decomposed by cycle number.
relatedConcepts: Partition of S_n by cycle count
